The question of whether pesticides are harmful to all insects is contested across the retrieved evidence. Many sources argue that most widely used pesticides are broad-spectrum and do not discriminate between species. [d1] states that "most of the widely used chemicals are broad spectrum, meaning they affect more than just the intended target pest," harming bees, butterflies, beetles, and other insects beyond the intended target. [d4] cites a European Academies Science Advisory Council report concluding that widespread pesticide use "has severe effects on a range of organisms" and that predatory insects like parasitic wasps and ladybugs are all harmed. [d8] reports a peer-reviewed study finding that "pesticides harmed beneficial soil invertebrates in 70.5 percent of cases reviewed," and [d2] notes that pesticide use kills "not only the targeted pests but also the natural predators and parasites of those pests." [d6] adds that even pesticides not intended for insects can harm them directly or indirectly, affecting reproduction and disease susceptibility. [d9] quotes a farmer acknowledging that "the toxin doesn't separate between the different insects."

However, other evidence challenges the claim that all pesticides harm all insects. [d5] (Clemson University Extension) explicitly states that insecticidal soaps are "among the safest pesticides" and that "most beneficial insects are not harmed by soap sprays." [d7] similarly argues that when used properly, neonicotinoids "effectively control problem insects, while exhibiting less impact on non-target insects (including bees)." These conflicting findings suggest that while many conventional pesticides pose broad risks to insects, certain pesticide types or application methods may spare beneficial species, and the degree of harm depends heavily on the specific chemical, its application, and the insect species involved.
